01-01.source_text: Sanwu Liji, Xu Zheng (Three Kingdoms, Wu); surviving passages quoted in Yiwen Leiju, vol. 1, and Taiping Yulan, vol. 2.
01-01.source_quote: Heaven and earth were a chaos like an egg, and Pangu was born within it. After eighteen thousand years they separated: the clear yang became heaven and the turbid yin became earth. Between them Pangu changed nine times each day, divine in heaven and sage upon earth. Each day heaven rose one zhang, earth thickened one zhang and Pangu grew one zhang. After another eighteen thousand years, heaven was exceedingly high, earth exceedingly deep and Pangu exceedingly tall.

01-02.source_text: Fengsu Tongyi, Huangba, vol. 1, Ying Shao (Eastern Han); in Wang Liqi's annotated edition.
01-02.source_quote: When heaven and earth had opened, there were no people. Nuwa kneaded yellow earth to make them. The task was too great for her strength, so she drew a cord through mud and lifted it to make people.

01-03.source_text: Huainanzi, Lanming Xun, Liu An (Western Han), with Gao You's commentary.
01-03.source_quote: In ancient times the four supports failed and the Nine Regions split. Heaven did not cover everything, nor did earth support everything. Fire burned without end and water surged without cease; fierce beasts devoured people and birds of prey seized the old and weak. Nuwa smelted five-colored stones to repair the sky, cut off a giant turtle's legs to raise the four supports, killed the black dragon to save Jizhou, and piled reed ash to stop the flood.

01-03-a.source_text: Huainanzi, Lanming Xun, Liu An (Western Han), with Gao You's commentary.
01-03-a.source_quote: Nuwa smelted five-colored stones to repair the azure sky.

01-03-b.source_text: Huainanzi, Lanming Xun, Liu An (Western Han), with Gao You's commentary.
01-03-b.source_quote: She cut off the giant turtle's legs to raise the four supports.

01-03-c.source_text: Huainanzi, Lanming Xun, Liu An (Western Han), with Gao You's commentary.
01-03-c.source_quote: She killed the black dragon to save Jizhou.

01-03-d.source_text: Huainanzi, Lanming Xun, Liu An (Western Han), with Gao You's commentary.
01-03-d.source_quote: She piled reed ash to stop the overflowing waters.

01-04.source_text: Huainanzi, Tianwen Xun, Liu An (Western Han), with Gao You's commentary.
01-04.source_quote: Gonggong contended with Zhuanxu for rulership. In anger he struck Mount Buzhou, breaking heaven's pillar and earth's bonds. Heaven tilted northwest, drawing the sun, moon and stars that way; earth sank in the southeast, drawing waters and dust toward it.

02-01.source_text: Zhouyi (Book of Changes), Xici II; Shisanjing Zhushu edition.
02-01.source_quote: When Fuxi ruled the world, he looked upward at heaven's patterns and downward at earth's forms. He observed the markings of birds and beasts and the conditions of the land, taking examples nearby from his own body and far away from other things. Thus he first created the eight trigrams to communicate divine powers and classify the nature of all things.

02-02.source_text: Fengsu Tongyi, Ying Shao (Eastern Han); Duyi Zhi, Li Rong (Tang), final volume.
02-02.source_quote: Nuwa was Fuxi's younger sister (Fengsu Tongyi). At the world's beginning only Nuwa and her brother lived on Mount Kunlun. They considered marrying but felt ashamed. They prayed that, if heaven intended their union, the smoke should join; otherwise it should scatter. The smoke joined (Duyi Zhi).
02-02.basis_note: No Shanhaijing place or direction supports this location. The marker indexes a chapter story; it does not identify an actual site or distance.

02-03.source_text: Huainanzi, Xiuwu Xun, Liu An (Western Han), with Gao You's commentary.
02-03.source_quote: Shennong tasted the flavors of the many herbs and encountered seventy poisons in a single day.

02-04.source_text: Hanfeizi, Wu Du, Han Fei (Warring States); Wang Xianshen's Hanfeizi Jijie.
02-04.source_quote: In ancient times people were few and beasts many. People ate fruits and shellfish, whose rawness and foul odors harmed their stomachs, and many became ill. A sage appeared who made fire by friction to cook away the rawness. The people rejoiced, made him ruler of the world and called him Suiren.

02-05.source_text: Hanfeizi, Wu Du, Han Fei (Warring States); Wang Xianshen's Hanfeizi Jijie.
02-05.source_quote: In ancient times people were few and beasts many; people could not withstand beasts, insects and snakes. A sage appeared who built wooden nests to escape these dangers. The people rejoiced, made him ruler of the world and called him Youchao.

03-01.source_text: Shiji, Wudi Benji, Sima Qian (Western Han); with the three commentaries.
03-01.source_quote: In Xuanyuan's time, Shennong's lineage declined. He fought the Yan Emperor on the plain of Banquan. After three battles he achieved his purpose.
03-01.basis_note: The Shiji describes the Yellow Emperor fighting the Yan Emperor at Banquan. Modern identifications differ; this marker establishes no candidate site, real direction or distance.

03-02.source_text: Shiji, Wudi Benji, Sima Qian (Western Han); with the three commentaries.
03-02.source_quote: Chiyou rebelled and refused the ruler's commands. The Yellow Emperor summoned the lords' armies and fought Chiyou on the plain of Zhuolu, capturing and killing him.
03-02.basis_note: The Shiji describes the Yellow Emperor fighting Chiyou at Zhuolu. Modern identifications differ; this marker establishes no candidate site, real direction or distance.

03-03.source_text: Shanhaijing, Beyond the Seas: West; Guo Pu commentary edition.
03-03.source_quote: Xingtian contended with the ruler for divine power. The ruler cut off his head and buried it at Mount Changyang. Xingtian then used his nipples as eyes and his navel as a mouth, wielding shield and axe in a dance.
03-03.basis_note: The text names Mount Changyang but provides no verifiable absolute coordinates. This is a narrative anchor.

03-04.source_text: Shanhaijing, Northern Mountains; Guo Pu commentary edition.
03-04.source_quote: Mount Fajiu has many cudrania trees. A bird there resembles a crow, with a patterned head, white beak and red feet. It is called Jingwei, and its cry speaks its own name. It was the Yan Emperor's youngest daughter, Nuwa, who drowned while visiting the Eastern Sea and never returned. She became Jingwei and constantly carried wood and stones from the western mountains to fill the Eastern Sea.
03-04.basis_note: Northern Mountains associates Jingwei with Mount Fajiu and describes carrying western wood and stones to the Eastern Sea. The diagram restates this relationship without absolute distances.
03-04.location_label: Mount Fajiu — Eastern Sea · relationship diagram

03-05.source_text: Shanhaijing, Beyond the Seas: North; Guo Pu commentary edition. Also see Great Wilderness: North.
03-05.source_quote: Kuafu raced after the sun and reached its setting place. Thirsty, he drank from the Yellow and Wei Rivers, but they were insufficient. He went north to drink from the Great Marsh. Before reaching it he died of thirst along the way. His abandoned staff became Deng Forest.
03-05.basis_note: The text describes pursuit, drinking from the two rivers, seeking the Great Marsh, death before arrival and the staff's transformation. Only narrative order is depicted.
03-05.location_label: Yellow and Wei Rivers — Great Marsh · narrative sequence

04-01.source_text: Huainanzi, Tianwen Xun, Liu An (Western Han), with Gao You's commentary.
04-01.source_quote: Gonggong contended with Zhuanxu for rulership. In anger he struck Mount Buzhou, breaking heaven's pillar and earth's bonds.
04-01.basis_note: Mount Buzhou has several proposed identifications. This marker aids reading rather than establishing real coordinates.

04-02.source_text: Huainanzi, Benjing Xun, Liu An (Western Han), with Gao You's commentary.
04-02.source_quote: In Yao's time ten suns rose together, scorching crops and killing plants, leaving people without food. Yayu, Zaochi, Jiuying, Dafeng, Fengxi and the long serpent harmed the people. Yao sent Yi to kill Zaochi in the wilds of Chouhua, Jiuying above the fierce waters, and Dafeng at Qingqiu's marsh. He shot upward at the ten suns and killed Yayu below, severed the long serpent at Dongting and captured Fengxi in the mulberry grove.
04-02.basis_note: The passage lists several actions and places together. This marker does not identify a single site or reconstruct a route.
04-02.location_label: Actions in several places · relationship diagram

04-03.source_text: Huainanzi, Lanming Xun, Liu An (Western Han), with Gao You's commentary.
04-03.source_quote: Yi obtained the elixir of immortality from the Queen Mother of the West. Heng'e stole it and fled to the moon; he felt bereft and had no way to replace it.
04-03.basis_note: The passage describes a mythical flight to the moon; it is not projected onto earthly coordinates.

04-04.source_text: Shanhaijing, Within the Seas; Guo Pu commentary edition.
04-04.source_quote: Floodwaters reached heaven. Without awaiting the ruler's command, Gun stole the ruler's growing earth to dam the flood. The ruler ordered Zhurong to kill Gun at Yujiao. Gun then brought forth Yu.
04-04.basis_note: The text places Gun's death at Yujiao, whose absolute location cannot be reliably established.

04-05.source_quote: Yao said: 'Shun, heaven's succession now rests upon you. Faithfully hold to the middle way. If the people of the four seas suffer hardship, heaven's favor will end forever.' Shun likewise charged Yu.
04-05.basis_note: The cited entry describes Yao charging Shun, without a specific place or direction suitable for map positioning.

05-01.source_text: Shangshu (Book of Documents), Yu Gong; Shisanjing Zhushu edition.
05-01.source_quote: Yu ordered the land, followed the mountains to clear trees, and established the great mountains and rivers.
05-01.basis_note: Flood control involves many waterways. This narrative anchor identifies no single event site, Nine Regions boundary, ancient riverbed or activity area.
05-01.location_label: Flood control in many places · narrative diagram

05-02.source_text: Shanhaijing, Beyond the Seas: North. Also compare Xiangyao in Great Wilderness: North.
05-02.source_quote: Gonggong's retainer Xiangliu had nine heads and fed upon nine mountains. Wherever he went became marshes and streams. Yu killed Xiangliu; his foul blood made the land unfit for grain. Yu tried to fill it, but it repeatedly collapsed, so he made it a terrace for the rulers, north of Kunlun and east of Rouli. Xiangliu had nine human faces and a blue-green serpent's body.
05-02.basis_note: This passage is from Beyond the Seas: North, rather than the Xiangyao entry in Great Wilderness: North. The rulers' terrace is described as north of Kunlun and east of Rouli, but this does not locate the killing or establish modern coordinates. Candidate sites and illustrations are not location evidence.

05-03.source_text: Shangshu (Book of Documents), Yi Ji; Shisanjing Zhushu edition.
05-03.source_quote: While engaged in this work, I married at Tushan, on the days xin, ren, gui and jia. Qi cried as a newborn, but I did not attend to him, devoting myself to planning the work on the land.
05-03.basis_note: Modern identifications of Tushan include Huaiyuan, Chongqing and Zhejiang. This anchor selects none of them and establishes no direction or distance relative to other events.

05-04.source_text: Hanshu, Wudi Ji; Yan Shigu's commentary quoting the Huainanzi. This passage is absent from the received Huainanzi.
05-04.source_quote: Yu controlled the flood and opened a way through Mount Huanyuan, transforming into a bear. He told the woman of Tushan to bring food when she heard the drum. Jumping upon a stone, he accidentally struck it. She came, saw him as a bear and fled in shame. At the foot of Mount Songgao she turned to stone while pregnant with Qi. Yu called, 'Give me my son.' The stone split on its north side, and Qi was born.
05-04.basis_note: This account survives in Yan Shigu's commentary, attributed to the Huainanzi, but is absent from its received text. The anchor does not locate the Qimu Stone or reconstruct the mountain.
05-04.location_label: Foot of Mount Songgao · narrative diagram

06-01.source_text: Zuo Zhuan, Duke Xiang, year 4; Shisanjing Zhushu edition.
06-01.source_quote: As Xia declined, Houyi moved from Chu to Qiongshi. Relying on Xia's people, he took over its government.

06-02.source_text: Zuo Zhuan, Duke Xiang, year 4; Shisanjing Zhushu edition.
06-02.source_quote: Han Zhuo was an unprincipled member of the Boming clan. Rejected by its ruler, he was taken in by Yi, trusted and made minister. Zhuo flattered those within and bribed those outside, deceiving the people while luring Yi into hunting. Through treachery he seized the state and won compliance within and without. Yi remained unrepentant; returning from the hunt, his household killed and cooked him.

06-03.source_text: Zuo Zhuan, Duke Ai, year 1; Shisanjing Zhushu edition.
06-03.source_quote: Jiao of Guo destroyed Zhen'guan, attacked Zhenxun and killed Xia's ruler Xiang. His pregnant wife Min escaped through a hole, returned to Youreng and bore Shaokang. As Youreng's official in charge of herds, he remained wary of Jiao. Pursued by Jiao's agent, he fled to Youyu and became chief cook. Yu Si married him to his two daughters and granted him Lun. With a tract of land and a company of followers, he cultivated virtue and planned to rally Xia's people and restore its officials.
06-03.location_label: Youreng, Youyu and Lun · migration narrative

06-04.source_text: Shiji, Xia Benji, Sima Qian (Western Han); with the three commentaries.
06-04.source_quote: Jie of Xia held a gathering at Reng, and Youmin rebelled. Jie defeated Youmin, thereby bringing about his state's ruin. He summoned Tang, imprisoned him at Xiatai and later released him.

06-05.source_text: Lushi Chunqiu, Benwei, Lu Buwei (Warring States), with Gao You's commentary.
06-05.source_quote: A woman of Youshen gathering mulberries found a baby in a hollow mulberry tree and offered him to her ruler, who ordered the cooks to raise him. Investigation revealed that his mother lived beside the Yi River. While pregnant, she dreamed a deity warning: 'When water emerges from the mortar, flee east and do not look back.' The next day water appeared; she warned her neighbors and fled ten li east, then looked back. Her town was submerged, and she became a hollow mulberry tree. Thus the child was named Yi Yin. He grew into a worthy man.

07-03.source_text: Mu Tianzi Zhuan (The Travels of King Mu), vol. 2; Guo Pu commentary edition.
07-03.source_quote: The Son of Heaven ascended Kunlun Hill to view the Yellow Emperor's palace and the burial of Fenglong, so that later generations might know of them.
07-03.basis_note: The episode is in volume 2. Modern identifications of Kunlun are disputed. This marker records the narrative rather than a mountain location or real itinerary.

07-01.source_text: Mu Tianzi Zhuan (The Travels of King Mu), vol. 3; Guo Pu commentary edition.
07-01.source_quote: On the auspicious jiazi day, the Son of Heaven visited the Queen Mother of the West, presenting a white gui tablet and a dark bi disk.
07-01.basis_note: This episode is in volume 3. Its Queen Mother is not conflated with figures described in different Shanhaijing books. Her country's location is disputed; the layout identifies no real site.

07-02.source_text: Mu Tianzi Zhuan (The Travels of King Mu), vol. 3; Guo Pu commentary edition.
07-02.source_quote: On the yichou day the Son of Heaven entertained the Queen Mother beside the Jade Pool. She sang: 'White clouds are in heaven; hills rise below. The way is distant, mountains and rivers divide us. May you live and return again.' He answered: 'I return to the eastern lands to bring peace to the Xia peoples. Once all are at ease, I shall see you again. Within three years I will return to your country.'
07-02.basis_note: The banquet follows the jiazi meeting on the next day, yichou, in volume 3. Identifications of the Jade Pool are disputed. No candidate lake, distance or itinerary is selected.

07-04.source_text: Mu Tianzi Zhuan (The Travels of King Mu), vol. 3; Guo Pu commentary edition.
07-04.source_quote: The Son of Heaven ascended Mount Yan, recorded his journey on its stone and planted a scholar tree.
07-04.basis_note: Volume 3 places this episode after the Jade Pool banquet. Mount Yan's location and the following inscription wording are uncertain. The marker selects no modern candidate or route; the illustration invents no inscription.

place-zhaoyao.source: Shanhaijing · Nanshan Jing (Sibu Congkan facsimile of the Ming Chenghua edition; Guo Pu commentary)
place-zhaoyao.editorial_note: The quotation is transcribed into simplified Chinese from the cited scan; punctuation is editorial. The ancient text, Guo Pu’s commentary and the project paraphrase are distinguished. Reported effects are ancient textual claims, not advice for use.
place-zhaoyao.name: Mount Zhaoyao
place-zhaoyao.description: Above the Western Sea, Mount Zhaoyao opens the Nanshan Jing. Cassia trees, metals and jade occur here. Zhuyu resembles chives and bears blue-green flowers; Migu has dark grain and shining blossoms. White-eared Shengsheng move low to the ground. The Li𪊨 River rises here and flows west to the sea, with an object called Yupei recorded in its waters.
place-zhaoyao.quote: Its first mountain is Zhaoyao, overlooking the Western Sea, with abundant cassia, metals and jade. A chive-like herb with blue-green flowers is called Zhuyu; eating it is said to prevent hunger. A tree resembling gu has dark grain and shining flowers; it is called Migu, and carrying it is said to prevent losing one’s way. An ape-like creature with white ears crouches and walks as a person does: Shengsheng. Eating it is said to aid running. The Li𪊨 River rises here and flows west to the sea. Its waters contain much Yupei; wearing it is said to prevent abdominal affliction.
place-zhaoyao.artwork_caption: Place scene · Mountain shape, vegetation and the depiction of water are artistic interpretations.
place-zhaoyao.direction: A textual place anchor within Nanshan Jing. Its diagram position does not represent modern coordinates, scaled distances or a continuous visitor route.

place-niuyang.source: Shanhaijing · Nanshan Jing (Sibu Congkan facsimile of the Ming Chenghua edition; Guo Pu commentary)
place-niuyang.editorial_note: The quotation is transcribed into simplified Chinese from the cited scan; punctuation is editorial. The ancient text, Guo Pu’s commentary and the project paraphrase are distinguished. Reported effects are ancient textual claims, not advice for use.
place-niuyang.name: Mount Niuyang
place-niuyang.description: The two faces of Mount Niuyang are described through their resources: red metal on the sunny side, white metal on the shaded side. Lushu has a white head, tiger markings, a red tail and a singing cry. The Guai River rises from the mountain and flows east into the Xianyi River. Xuangui is described in this water passage, as the account turns from the mountain toward its downstream waters.
place-niuyang.quote: Another 370 li east is Mount Niuyang. Its sunny side has red metal; its shaded side has white metal. A horse-like creature has a white head, tiger markings, a red tail and a singing cry. It is called Lushu; wearing it is said to favor descendants. The Guai River rises here and flows east into the Xianyi River. These waters contain many dark turtles with bird heads and serpent tails, called Xuangui. Their cry resembles splitting wood; wearing them is said to prevent deafness and treat ailments.
place-niuyang.artwork_caption: Place scene · Mountain shape, vegetation and the depiction of water are artistic interpretations.
place-niuyang.direction: A textual place anchor within Nanshan Jing. Its diagram position does not represent modern coordinates, scaled distances or a continuous visitor route.

place-qingqiu.source: Shanhaijing · Nanshan Jing (Sibu Congkan facsimile of the Ming Chenghua edition; Guo Pu commentary)

place-qingqiu.name: Mount Qingqiu
place-qingqiu.description: Jade occurs on Qingqiu’s sunny side, and a green mineral is recorded on its shaded side. Its fox has nine tails and an infant-like cry. Guanguan is a dove-like bird whose call is likened to people calling to one another. The Ying River rises here and flows south into Jiyi Marsh. Chiru, with fish bodies and human faces, are described in this water passage.
place-qingqiu.quote: Another 300 li east is Mount Qingqiu. Its sunny side has jade; its shaded side has green mineral. A fox-like creature has nine tails and an infant-like cry. It can eat people; eating it is said to ward off gu. A dove-like bird calls as if calling out; its name is Guanguan, and wearing it is said to prevent bewilderment. The Ying River rises here and flows south into Jiyi Marsh. These waters contain Chiru, with fish bodies, human faces and mandarin-duck-like calls. Eating them is said to prevent skin disease.

The text says eating it prevents hunger; this records an ancient claim, not an identification of a present-day edible plant.

plant-migu.name: Migu
plant-migu.description: Migu is a tree on Mount Zhaoyao. It resembles gu, has dark grain and flowers that shine all around. Guo Pu explains gu as paper mulberry. The claim that carrying Migu prevents losing one’s way belongs to the ancient account; no modern species identification is asserted here.

passage-nanshan-zhaoyao.name: Mount Zhaoyao
passage-nanshan-zhaoyao.description: Cassia, herbs and an unusual tree open the account above the Western Sea.
passage-nanshan-zhaoyao.quote: The Southern Mountains begin with the Que range. Its first mountain, Zhaoyao, overlooks the Western Sea and has cassia, metals and jade. Zhuyu resembles chives and has blue-green flowers; eating it is said to prevent hunger. Migu resembles gu, has dark grain and shining flowers; carrying it is said to prevent losing the way. Shengsheng resembles an ape with white ears, crouching and walking like a person; eating it is said to aid running. The Li𪊨 River flows west to the sea, with Yupei said to prevent abdominal affliction when worn.

passage-nanshan-di.description: Lu combines the account’s categories of fish and land-dwelling form.
passage-nanshan-di.quote: Three hundred li east is the fifth mountain, with much water but no vegetation. A fish called Lu resembles an ox, lives on land, has a serpent tail and wings beneath its flanks, and has a bovine-like cry; the precise comparison includes an unresolved image glyph. The nine excerpts and sources remain distinct; no source, complete course or modern confluence is inferred.

These are excerpts from seven separate passages. The Chu rises and flows south into the Wei, in the separate Shuli passage. The Jing rises and flows east into the Wei in the separate Gao passage.

Conglong has a sheep-like form and red mane; Min resembles a cui bird with a red beak.

Conglong resembles a sheep with a red mane. Min resembles a cui bird with a red beak and is said to ward off fire.

The Yu flows north into the Shao; its water account names turtle-shaped Bangyu with a sheep-like voice. Zuoniu and Qianyang are also listed. The quail-like, yellow-bodied, red-beaked Feiyi here is a bird, separate from Taihua’s snake.

A bird called Feiyi resembles a quail, with a yellow body and red beak; eating it is said to relieve li and kill parasites.

Xiao is monkey-like with long arms and a skill for throwing. Tuofei is owl-like, with a human face and one foot, appearing in winter and dormant in summer. Wearing its feathers is explained separately in the commentary.

Tuofei resembles an owl, with a human face and one foot; it appears in winter and lies dormant in summer. Wearing it is said to remove fear of thunder.

passage-xishan-tiandi.name: Mount Tiandi
passage-xishan-tiandi.description: Three hundred and fifty li west of Bozhong is Tiandi, with zong and nan above, and jian and hui below. Xibian is dog-shaped. The quail-like Li has black markings and a red feather tuft below the head, following the commentary on weng. Duheng resembles kui and smells like miwu. Two interpretations of its horse-related claim remain commentary; the mountain name does not establish a divine residence.
passage-xishan-tiandi.quote: Three hundred and fifty li west is Mount Tiandi, with zong and nan above and jian and hui below. A dog-shaped beast is called Xibian; using its hide as a mat is said to protect against gu. A quail-shaped bird with black markings and red weng, glossed as feathers below the head, is called Li; eating it is said to relieve hemorrhoids. An herb shaped like kui and smelling like miwu is called Duheng. The text says it can help with horses, and that eating it relieves neck swellings; the horse claim has two commentary interpretations.

passage-xishan-gaotu.name: Mount Gaotu
passage-xishan-gaotu.description: Three hundred and eighty li southwest of Tiandi is Gaotu. The Se flows west into Zhuzi, while the Tu flows south into Jihuo; these remain separate waters. Se follows Guo Pu’s pronunciation gloss. Dansu, silver, gold and gui trees are listed separately. The white stone Yu and herb Wutiao have separate mouse-poisoning claims. Yingru is deer-shaped with a white tail, horse feet, human hands and four horns; commentary assigns the hands to the front feet. Shusi is chi-shaped with human feet.
passage-xishan-gaotu.quote: Three hundred and eighty li southwest is Mount Gaotu. The Se rises here and flows west into the Zhuzi; the Tu rises here and flows south into the Jihuo. Dansu occurs on its sunny side, silver and gold on its shaded side, and gui trees above. A white stone called Yu is said to poison mice. Wutiao resembles gaoyou, with kui-like leaves and red undersides, and is also said to poison mice. A deer-shaped beast with a white tail, horse feet, human hands and four horns is called Yingru. A chi-shaped bird with human feet is called Shusi. Eating it is said to relieve neck swellings; commentary records an alternative ailment character.

Explanations of zhong, tailao and yu-jade belong to Guo Pu’s commentary. No deity appearance or ritual scene is invented. The final difficult wording on zhu, bai di and patterned borders is retained without silently emending it.

The text then describes the Yu rite, zhu, a hundred-day observance, offerings counted in hundreds, yu-jade, wine, gui and bi jades. The other seventeen mountains receive one sheep each. The concluding wording on zhu, bai di and patterned borders is retained with the edition commentary rather than given a speculative fluent translation.

passage-xishan-chongwu.name: Mount Chongwu
passage-xishan-chongwu.description: Chongwu opens the third Western range, south of the He, with four named landmarks in view. An unnamed tree has round leaves, white fu, red flowers, dark markings and zhi-like fruit. Jufu resembles a yu with patterned arms; the edition’s bao hu wording is retained. Manman resembles a fu bird but has one wing and one eye and flies in pairs; its appearance is linked to flooding.
passage-xishan-chongwu.quote: The third Western range begins at Mount Chongwu, south of the He. It overlooks Zhongsui to the north, Yao Marsh to the south, the Emperor’s Tuan Beast Hill to the west and Yan Pool to the east. An unnamed tree has round leaves, white fu, red flowers, dark markings and fruit like zhi; eating it is said to favor descendants. Jufu resembles a yu with patterned arms and the wording bao hu, and is skilled at throwing. Manman resembles a fu bird, has one wing and one eye, and can fly when paired; its appearance is said to herald great floods throughout the land.
passage-xishan-chongwu.content_note: Unit162 begins on scan51 although captured as52; units163–168 are on52 and169 begins Changsha. The image-glyph marker labelled bo is restored as tuan in the reading quotation from the scan, while captured text is unchanged. The bao hu wording for Jufu remains as printed, without silently substituting a leopard tail or importing the sun-chasing Kuafu story. The tree gloss spans units164–165 and retains uncertain captured wording; Manman coloration and the Jianjian comparison belong to commentary.

The Dan flows west into Ji Marsh, with white jade and jade paste in the water account. The text also records 460 li of wetlands between Mi and Zhong, with unnamed wondrous birds, strange beasts and wondrous fish.
passage-xishan-mishan.quote: Four hundred and twenty li northwest is Mount Mi. Danmu has round leaves, red stems, yellow flowers and red fruit, tastes like malt sugar and is said to prevent hunger. The Dan River rises here and flows west into Ji Marsh, with white jade and surging jade paste. Huangdi consumes the paste, which produces xuan jade and waters the danmu; after five years its colors clear and flavors become fragrant. Huangdi takes Mi’s jade blossom and casts it onto Zhong’s sunny side. Jinyu jade is prized for its texture, luster and five colors. Heaven, earth, ghosts and spirits partake of it; gentlemen wear it to ward off ill fortune. Between Mi and Zhong are 460 li of wetlands with wondrous birds, strange beasts and wondrous fish.

An unnamed emperor executes them, in an account continuing to Yao Cliff east of Zhong. Qinpi becomes a great e bird and Gu a jun bird, with separate forms and omens of warfare and drought. place-xishan-zhongshan.quote: In the separate Mi passage, Huangdi casts jade blossom onto Zhong’s sunny side, and 460 li of wetlands lie between Mi and Zhong. Four hundred and twenty li northwest is Mount Zhong. Its child is called Gu, with a human face and dragon body. With Qinpi, Gu kills Baojiang on Kunlun’s sunny side. The emperor executes them; east of Zhong is Yao Cliff. Qinpi becomes a great e bird, like a diao, with black markings, a white head, red beak and tiger claws; its voice resembles a chenhu, and its appearance heralds war. Gu becomes a jun bird, like a chi, with red feet, a straight beak, yellow markings and white head; its voice resembles a hu, and its appearance brings drought to that settlement.

passage-xishan-zhongshan.name: Mount Zhong
passage-xishan-zhongshan.description: Four hundred and twenty li northwest of Mi is Zhong. Gu has a human face and dragon body; with Qinpi, Gu kills Baojiang on Kunlun’s sunny side. An unnamed emperor executes them, in an account continuing to Yao Cliff east of Zhong. Qinpi becomes a great e bird and Gu a jun bird, with separate forms and omens of warfare and drought. The final King Mu account and its animals remain commentary, including annotation-only units.
passage-xishan-zhongshan.quote: Four hundred and twenty li northwest is Mount Zhong. Its child is called Gu, with a human face and dragon body. With Qinpi, Gu kills Baojiang on Kunlun’s sunny side. The emperor executes them; east of Zhong is Yao Cliff. Qinpi becomes a great e bird, like a diao, with black markings, a white head, red beak and tiger claws; its voice resembles a chenhu, and its appearance heralds war. Gu becomes a jun bird, like a chi, with red feet, a straight beak, yellow markings and white head; its voice resembles a hu, and its appearance brings drought to that settlement.
passage-xishan-zhongshan.content_note: Units193–202 span scans55–56; unit198 is on55 despite capture as56. Units201–202 contain only the King Mu commentary and are retained. Gu’s name gloss and the chenhu gloss continue across units. The Li Mountain comparison and a missing captured character remain commentary issues. Qinpi’s original appearance is unspecified; each transformation is a separate linked form. Bao’s variant is commentary and the emperor is not identified as Huangdi. Zhong retains its stable ID and both Mi and Zhong sources, with 460 and 420 li kept separate. King Mu’s animals are not added as main-text creatures.

passage-xishan-huaijiang.name: Mount Huaijiang
passage-xishan-huaijiang.description: Three hundred and twenty li west of Taiqi is Huaijiang. The Qiushi flows north into the You, with luomu in its waters; goods above and on opposing slopes are recorded separately. Yingzhao oversees the emperor’s level garden, with a horse’s body, human face, tiger markings and bird wings. Views extend to Kunlun, Houji’s Great Marsh, Zhupi and a four-tiered mountain in the eastern view. The closing water and an unnamed ox-like deity with eight feet, two heads and a horse’s tail form a separate account.
passage-xishan-huaijiang.quote: Three hundred and twenty li west is Mount Huaijiang. The Qiushi River rises here and flows north into the You, containing many luomu. Above are qing xionghuang and hidden langgan, gold and jade; the sunny side has dansu and the shaded side the wording cai huangjin yin. This is the emperor’s level garden, overseen by Yingzhao, who has a horse’s body, human face, tiger markings and bird wings, circles the four seas and sounds like liu. To the south is luminous Kunlun; to the west the Great Marsh where Houji remains hidden, with jade and the yaomu zhi you ruo wording on its shaded side. To the north is Zhupi, inhabited by Huai-gui Lilun and ying and zhan birds. To the east is a four-tiered mountain in the eastern view, where Youqiong spirits dwell, each on a mountain side. There is clear flowing water and an ox-like heavenly deity with eight feet, two heads and a horse’s tail, sounding like bohuang; its appearance is an omen of warfare in that settlement.
passage-xishan-huaijiang.content_note: Units208–222 span scans57–58; unit216 is on57 despite capture as58. Four image-glyph markers are restored only in the reading quotation, with the capture retained. Kunlun’s southern view and main passage share a stable mountain ID while retaining separate sources. Namesake You and Zhupi references retain separate sources, without merging You Marsh.

place-xishan-kunlun.name: Kunlun Hill
place-xishan-kunlun.description: Four hundred li southwest is Kunlun, the emperor’s lower capital. Luwu has a tiger body, nine tails, a human face and tiger claws, overseeing the nine heavenly divisions and the seasons of the imperial garden. Tulou resembles a four-horned sheep and eats people. Qinyuan resembles a bee as large as a mandarin duck; its sting kills birds and beasts and withers trees. Chun birds oversee the emperor’s equipment. Shatang resembles tang, with yellow flowers and red, plum-flavored, seedless fruit; eating it is said to prevent drowning. Pin grass resembles kui and tastes like scallion; eating it relieves fatigue. The He flows south, then east to Wuda; the Chi southeast to Fantian’s water; the Yang southwest to Choutu’s water; the Hei west to Dayu. Many strange birds and beasts occur here.

passage-xishan-yushan.name: Mount Yu
passage-xishan-yushan.description: Three hundred and fifty li west is Mount Yu, home of Xiwangmu. She is human-shaped, with a leopard tail and tiger teeth, a powerful whistle, disheveled hair and a sheng headdress, overseeing heavenly calamities and the five destructive forces. Jiao resembles a dog with leopard markings and ox-like horns, sounds like a barking dog, and its appearance foretells a plentiful year. Shengyu is a red, zhai-shaped bird that eats fish and sounds like lu; its appearance foretells flooding.

passage-xishan-zhange.name: Mount Zhange
passage-xishan-zhange.description: Two hundred and eighty li west is Zhange, without vegetation, rich in yaobi and unusual things. Zheng resembles a red leopard with five tails and one horn, sounding like struck stones. Bifang resembles a crane, with one foot, red markings, a blue-green body and a white beak. It calls its own name; its appearance foretells an uncanny fire in the settlement.

passage-xishan-yiwang.name: Mount Yiwang
passage-xishan-yiwang.description: Traveling west by water for a hundred li reaches Yiwang, without vegetation and rich in gold and jade. Huan resembles a li with one eye and three tails, producing a multitude of sounds; it is said to ward off harm and relieve jaundice when worn or consumed. Qiyu resembles a crow with three heads and six tails and laughs readily; wearing or consuming it is said to prevent nightmares and ward off harm.

passage-xishan-zhongqu.description: Three hundred li west is Zhongqu. Jade occurs on the sunny side; xionghuang, white jade and gold on the shaded side. Bo resembles a horse with a white body, black tail, one horn and tiger teeth and claws, sounding like a drum. It eats tigers and leopards and is said to ward off weapons. Huai trees resemble tang, with round leaves and red fruit as large as mugua fruit; eating the fruit is said to increase strength.

passage-xishan-niaoshu.name: Mount Niaoshu Tongxue
passage-xishan-niaoshu.description: Two hundred and twenty li west is Niaoshu Tongxue, with many white tigers and white jade. The Wei flows east into the He and contains Saoyu, resembling zhan fish; their movement foretells warfare. The Lan rises on the western side and flows west into the Han, containing Rupi fish, shaped like overturned pans with bird heads, fish fins and fish tails. They sound like struck chimes and stones and produce pearls and jade. Details of birds and mice sharing holes belong to commentary.

passage-xishan-yanzi.name: Mount Yanzi
passage-xishan-yanzi.description: Three hundred and sixty li southwest is Yanzi. Dan trees have gu-like leaves and melon-sized fruit, with red outer coloring and black markings; eating them is said to relieve jaundice and ward off fire. Turtles occur on the sunny side and jade on the shaded side. The Tiao flows west into the sea and contains whetstones. Shuhu has a horse body, bird wings, a human face and a snake tail, and likes lifting people. Another bird resembles a xiao but has a human face, wei-like body and dog tail; its name follows its cry, without a captured name, and its appearance foretells drought.

passage-beishan-qiuru.name: Mount Qiuru
passage-beishan-qiuru.description: Qiuru lies 250 li north of Danhu, with copper above and jade below but no vegetation. The Hua rises here and flows west into the Zhupi. Huayu resembles an eel with a red back; Shuima is horse-shaped, with patterned forelegs and an ox tail. The foreleg reading comes from Guo Pu, whose older quotations and Han account remain commentary rather than additional anatomy.
passage-beishan-qiuru.quote: Two hundred and fifty li north is Mount Qiuru, with copper above, jade below, and no grasses or trees. The Hua River rises here and flows west into the Zhupi. Huayu is eel-shaped with a red back and a sound compared to wu; eating it is said to relieve warts. Shuima is horse-shaped, with patterned forelegs and an ox tail; its sound resembles a call.
passage-beishan-qiuru.content_note: Units 5–9 are on scan 76; unit 9 was captured as 77 and is corrected only in the reading page index. Unit 10 continues the call on 77; unit 11 begins Dai. The wu pronunciation in unit 8 belongs to the preceding fish sound, and the wart gloss to its eating claim. Mount Zhupi appears only in commentary and remains separate from its Western namesake. The Zhouli black-spine comparison does not add a black back to Shuima; incomplete or variant captured commentary is retained without claiming a critical edition.
passage-beishan-qiuru.commentary_quote: Guo Pu says that the receiving river rises at Mount Zhupi; the eel resembles a snake; wu resembles the sound of people resisting one another, with a pronunciation gloss. Warts are glossed separately. For Shuima, bi means forelegs; the commentary quotes older horse wording and a Han-era account. Its call is compared to a human shout.

place-beishan-qiuru.commentary_quote: Guo Pu says that the receiving river rises at Mount Zhupi; the eel resembles a snake; wu resembles the sound of people resisting one another, with a pronunciation gloss. The Zhouli black-spine comparison does not add a black back to Shuima; incomplete or variant captured commentary is retained without claiming a critical edition.

passage-beishan-daishan.name: Mount Dai
passage-beishan-daishan.description: Dai lies 300 li north of Qiuru, with jade above and qingbi below. Huanshu is horse-shaped with one plated horn; Qiyu is crow-shaped, five-colored with red markings, and described as being male and female in itself. The Peng flows west into the Pihu, whose water account records red-feathered, chicken-shaped Youyu with three tails, six feet and four heads. The commentary treats horn plates, the namesake bird and pronunciation separately.
passage-beishan-daishan.quote: Three hundred li north is Mount Dai, with jade above and qingbi below. Huanshu is horse-shaped, with one horn bearing plates, and is said to ward off fire. Qiyu is crow-shaped, five-colored with red markings, being male and female in itself; eating it is said to prevent sores. The Peng rises here and flows west into the Pihu. Youyu is chicken-shaped with red feathers, three tails, six feet and four heads; it sounds like a magpie and eating it is said to relieve worry.
passage-beishan-daishan.content_note: Units 11–16 are on scan 77; 17 begins Qiaoming. The horn-plate gloss remains commentary. Qiyu’s namesake note continues across units 13–14, without merging it with the Western three-headed six-tailed bird. Youyu follows the pronunciation gloss; its chicken form is retained.

passage-beishan-qiaoming.name: Mount Qiaoming
passage-beishan-qiaoming.description: Qiaoming lies 400 li north of Dai. The Qiao flows west into the He and contains Heluo, with one head and ten bodies, sounding like a barking dog. Menghuai resembles huan with red bristles; Guo Pu glosses huan as a porcupine. The mountain has no vegetation and records qing xionghuang, with a qingbi variant kept separately.
passage-beishan-qiaoming.quote: Four hundred li north is Mount Qiaoming. The Qiao rises here and flows west into the He. Heluo fish have one head and ten bodies, sound like barking dogs, and are said to relieve swellings when eaten. Menghuai resembles huan with red bristles, sounds like liuliu, and is said to ward off misfortune. The mountain has no grasses or trees and much qing xionghuang.
passage-beishan-qiaoming.content_note: Units 17–18 are at the end of scan 77, despite 18 being captured as 78; 19–21 are on 78. The porcupine reading comes from commentary. Qing xionghuang spans a captured line break and remains one uncertain expression; its qingbi variant is not substituted into the main text.

passage-beishan-zhuoguang.description: Zhuoguang lies 350 li north of Qiaoming. The Xiao flows west into the He. Xixi is magpie-shaped with ten wings and scales at feather tips. Pines and bai trees grow above, zong and jiang below; lingyang and Fan are named. Guo Pu calls Fan uncertain and offers an owl comparison, retained without borrowing another mountain’s owl illustration.

The Xiao rises here and flows west into the He, containing Xixi fish shaped like magpies with ten wings and scales at feather tips. They sound like magpies and are said to ward off fire and prevent illness when eaten. Pines and bai trees grow above, zong and jiang below; lingyang and Fan are abundant.

passage-beishan-manlian.name: Mount Manlian
passage-beishan-manlian.description: Manlian lies 200 li north of Bianchun and has no vegetation. Zuzi is monkey-like, with a mane, ox tail, patterned arms and horse hooves, calling on seeing people. Jiao lives and flies in groups, has female-pheasant-like plumage and calls its own name; its eating claim is ancient.
passage-beishan-manlian.quote: Two hundred li north is Mount Manlian, without grasses or trees. Zuzi resembles a monkey, with a mane, ox tail, patterned arms and horse hooves; it calls on seeing people and cries its own name. Jiao lives and flies in groups, with plumage like a female pheasant; it calls its name and eating it is said to relieve wind illness.

Difficult characters in the captured pronunciation/variant gloss remain unresolved.

passage-beishan-danzhang.name: Mount Danzhang
passage-beishan-danzhang.description: Danzhang lies 180 li north of Manlian, without vegetation. Zhujian is leopard-shaped with a long tail, human head, ox ears and one eye; it roars, holds its tail while walking and coils it at rest. Baiye is pheasant-shaped, with a patterned head, white wings and yellow feet. The Li flows south into the Gang.
passage-beishan-danzhang.quote: One hundred and eighty li north is Mount Danzhang, without grasses or trees. Zhujian is leopard-shaped with a long tail, human head, ox ears and one eye. It roars, holds its tail while walking and coils it at rest. Baiye is pheasant-shaped, with a patterned head, white wings and yellow feet; eating it is said to relieve throat pain and chi illness. The Li rises here and flows south into the Gang.

The throat gloss spans captured units. Chi remains an ancient gloss rather than a modern diagnosis. The Li flows south, not west.

passage-beishan-dunhong.name: Mount Dunhong
passage-beishan-dunhong.description: Dunhong lies 320 li north of Daxian, with zong and nan above and zicao below. The Dunhong flows west into Youze, followed by an account of the northeastern corner of Kunlun and a source of the He. Red Gui fish, Si, Maoniu and Shijiu retain local records without borrowing forms from other mountains or treating the ancient source claim as modern geography.

The account speaks of the northeastern corner of Kunlun as a source of the He. Red Gui fish are abundant in the water; Si and Maoniu beasts and Shijiu birds are abundant on the mountain.

Gui follows the pronunciation gloss continuing into unit 71, not a modern salmon identification. The ancient source wording and commentary stay separate. passage-beishan-range1-summary.description: The first range runs from Danhu to Di, reporting 25 mountains and 5,490 li; 25 named mountain passages are present. Its deities have human faces and serpent bodies. The rites mention a cock, a pig, a gui tablet, burial and no ritual grain; Guo Pu explains burial of animal offerings and jade without rice. The northern raw-food account remains an ancient statement.

Its deities all have human faces and serpent bodies. The offering wording records one cock, a pig, burial and ji; one gui jade tablet is buried, without ritual grain. People north of these mountains all eat raw, uncooked things.

Banmao is crow-shaped with a human face, flying at night and resting by day; eating it is said to relieve heat illness. The Cen rises here and flows east into Qiongze.

passage-beishan-taihang.name: Mount Taihang
passage-beishan-taihang.description: The third Northern range opens with Taihang, whose head is called Gui. Gui has gold and jade above and bi below. Hui is antelope-like with four horns, a horse tail and spurs; Fen is magpie-shaped, white-bodied, red-tailed and six-legged.
passage-beishan-taihang.quote: The third Northern range begins with Mount Taihang; its head is called Mount Gui. Gold and jade occur above, bi below. passage-beishan-yangshan.name: Mount Yang

Xiangshe is five-colored and female-pheasant-shaped. The Liu flows south into the He; Xianfu has a fish head and pig body.
passage-beishan-yangshan.quote: Three hundred li east is Mount Yang, with jade above and gold and copper below. Separately, the Xianyu rises at Shi and flows south into Hutuo.

passage-beishan-range3-summary.name: Third Northern range summary and rites
passage-beishan-range3-summary.description: The third Northern range runs from Taihang to Wufeng: forty-six mountains and twelve thousand three hundred and fifty li. Twenty deities have horse bodies and human faces; their rites use the recorded yi zao zhi with burial. Fourteen have pig bodies carrying jade; their rites use jade without burial. Ten have pig bodies, eight feet and snake tails; their rites use one bi with burial. In all, forty-four deities are worshipped with tu grain and rice offerings, described as not fire-eating.
passage-beishan-range3-summary.quote: The third Northern range runs from Taihang to Wufeng: forty-six mountains and twelve thousand three hundred and fifty li. Twenty deities have horse bodies and human faces; their rites use the recorded yi zao zhi with burial. Fourteen have pig bodies carrying jade; their rites use jade without burial. Ten have pig bodies, eight feet and snake tails; their rites use one bi with burial. In all, forty-four deities are worshipped with tu grain and rice offerings, described as not fire-eating.
passage-beishan-range3-summary.content_note: Units 290–296 are on scan 108. Reported 46 and 47 named reading passages differ. The zhi pronunciation and no-burial jade glosses span units; ritual jade is not an anatomical gloss. The deity groups total 44, not a mountain count.

Tongtong resembles a piglet, has pearls and calls its name; the depicted loose pearl’s count and position are artistic. passage-dongshan-range1-summary.description: The first range runs from Suzhu to Zhu and reports twelve mountains and 3,600 li. Its gods have human bodies and dragon heads. passage-dongshan-kongsang-east.name: Mount Kongsang (Eastern second range)
passage-dongshan-kongsang-east.description: Kongsang opens the second Eastern range, facing Shi water northward, Ju Wu eastward, Shaling southward and Min marsh westward. Lingling is ox-shaped with tiger patterns and a qin-like sound, calling its name; its flood omen is ancient. The yin variant belongs to the sound and ling to the name. Instrument wood is commentary, without an identified tree species.
passage-dongshan-kongsang-east.quote: The second Eastern range begins at Mount Kongsang, facing Shi water to the north, Ju Wu to the east, Shaling to the south and Min marsh to the west. Lingling resembles an ox with tiger patterns, sounds like qin and calls its own name; its appearance is said to bring a great flood.
passage-dongshan-kongsang-east.content_note: Units 37–40 are on scan 113. Four directions remain distinct; this mountain is not merged with Northern Kongsang. Shared Shi water records another textual context, not a surveyed river.

Qiuyu is rabbit-like with a bird beak, kite eyes and a snake tail; the main text says it sleeps on seeing people, while commentary explains feigned death. No armor is borrowed from the modern armadillo namesake. The insect-damage omen remains an ancient account without invented species.

passage-dongshan-zhenshan.name: Mount Zhen
passage-dongshan-zhenshan.description: Five hundred li south is Mount Zhen, facing Zhen water to the south and Hu marsh to the east. Youyou resembles a horse with sheep eyes, four horns and an ox tail, and sounds like a howling dog; its appearance is said to bring crafty guests. Jiegou resembles a duck with a rat tail and climbs trees; its appearance is said to bring epidemics. Units 75–78 are on scan 117. Four horns, sheep eyes and ox tail belong to Youyou; the dog is a sound comparison. Jiegou has no human feet or rat head.

passage-dongshan-range2-summary.description: The second Eastern range, from Kongsang to Zhen, comprises seventeen mountains and 6,640 li. Its gods all have beast bodies, human faces and antlers. passage-dongshan-range3-summary.name: Third-range summary and rites
passage-dongshan-range3-summary.description: The third Eastern range, from Shihu to Wugao, is stated to comprise nineteen mountains and 6,900 li. Its gods all have human bodies and sheep horns. The offering uses one ram and millet; their appearance is said to bring damaging wind, rain and flood. Units 106–108 are all on scan 120. The facsimile says nineteen although only nine mountain accounts are named. The ten-mountain difference and the millet character are preserved; sheep horns do not make a sheep head.

passage-dongshan-beihao.name: Mount Beihao
passage-dongshan-beihao.description: The fourth Eastern range begins at Mount Beihao beside the Northern Sea. An unnamed tree resembles poplar, has red flowers and jujube-like fruit without pits; its flavor and eating claim are ancient accounts. The Shi rises here and flows northeast into the sea. Xieju resembles a wolf with a red head and rat eyes and sounds like a pig. Qique resembles a chicken with a white head, rat feet and tiger claws; both are described as eating people. Units 109–113 are on scan 121. The tree is not named as a jujube tree. The Northern Sea and the generic sea recipient remain separate textual names. Shared Shi water does not settle modern geographic identity; sound does not add a pig head.

passage-dongshan-dongshi.name: Mount Dongshi
passage-dongshan-dongshi.description: Three hundred and twenty li south is Mount Dongshi, with much cang jade above. A tree called Qi resembles poplar, has red grain and blood-like sap and bears no fruit; its horse-taming use is an ancient claim. The Ci rises here and flows northeast into the sea, with fine shells and Zi fish. Zi resembles crucian carp with one head and ten bodies, smells like miwu and is said to prevent flatulence when eaten. Unit 117 is actually at the end of scan 121; 118–121 are on 122. The horse gloss spans 118–119. The tree stays separate from the similarly written Yu-e plant; one head and ten bodies are mandatory, with no odor-derived organs.

passage-zhongshan-r01-gancao.name: Mount Ganzao
passage-zhongshan-r01-gancao.description: Ganzao opens the Bo range. Gong water flows west into the He. Tuo plant anatomy and ancient eating claims remain separate from the Nuo account. Guo Pu says the compared shu form is unknown, so Nuo retains a placeholder, without a modern rodent identification or a bear inferred from a variant character.
passage-zhongshan-r01-gancao.quote: The Central account begins with Mount Ganzao in the Bo range. Gong water rises here and flows west into the He. Niu trees are abundant above. Tuo has a mallow-like base, apricot-like leaves, yellow flowers and podded fruit, and is said to relieve dim sight. Nuo resembles a named shu with a patterned forehead and is said to relieve swellings when eaten.

passage-zhongshan-r01-lier.description: Li-er lies twenty li east of Ganzao. The square stems, round leaves, yellow flowers, hairiness and jian-like fruit describe Li, not the separately named Jiang tree. passage-zhongshan-r01-summary.name: First-range summary and rites
passage-zhongshan-r01-summary.description: The first range from Ganzao to Gudeng is stated to contain fifteen mountains and 6,670 li. Li-er has a distinguished rite; the other thirteen mountains use one sheep and a buried sangfeng tablet, without grain. The reported numbers remain even where their relationship is unclear. The mulberry tablet has a square lower part, pointed upper part, a central hole and metal decoration; these are ritual details, not deity anatomy.

passage-zhongshan-r03-aoan.description: The third Central range begins at Mount Ao-an, with tufu jade on its sunny side and ochre and gold on its shaded side. Helin and the qian/ju comparison remain uncertain; no body is invented for Xunchi. Four independent horns are mandatory for Fuzhu.

passage-zhongshan-r03-qingyao.description: Ten li east is Mount Qingyao, a secluded capital of the emperor, looking north toward a bend of the He and south toward Shanzhu, the transformation site of Yu’s father. Wuluo has a human face, leopard markings, a slim waist, white teeth and pierced ears with ju ornaments. Zhen water flows north into the He and has Yao birds, duck-like with blue-green bodies, red eyes and red tails. Xun grass is also described. The long account keeps deity, animals, plants and commentary separate. Jia bird is uncertain; snail/insect identifications are commentary. Human body details and the ju ornament shape are artistic. Unit 81 is on scan 10; 82–84 on 11.

Wuluo has a human face, leopard markings, a slim waist, white teeth and pierced ears with ju ornaments. Zhen water flows north into the He and has Yao birds, duck-like with blue-green bodies, red eyes and red tails. Xun grass is also described. The long account keeps deity, animals, plants and commentary separate. Jia bird is uncertain; snail/insect identifications are commentary. Human body details and the ju ornament shape are artistic. Unit 81 is on scan 10; 82–84 on 11.

passage-zhongshan-r05-summary.name: Fifth-range summary and rites
passage-zhongshan-r05-summary.description: The fifth range reports sixteen mountains and 2,982 li from Goulin to Yangxu. Sheng has a distinguished grand rite; Shou has rice, dark offerings, malt drink, shield dance and drum rites. The Shi-water rite mentions a black dog above, a hen below and a ewe blood offering. The sixteen-versus-fifteen difference is retained. These are ancient ritual records, not new deity anatomy or violent illustrations. The missing zhong marker is restored only in the reading layer.

passage-zhongshan-r06-yanghua.name: Mount Yanghua
passage-zhongshan-r06-yanghua.description: Ninety li west is Mount Yanghua, with gold and jade on its sunny side, green xionghuang on its shaded side, shuyu and kuxin plants. Yang water flows southwest into the Luo; Men water flows northeast into the He, while Jigu water rises on the shaded side and flows east into Men water. Copper is abundant above. The separate seven-hundred-and-ninety-li Men-water statement is retained even where its relationship to the earlier direction is unclear. Ancient eating claims and the black-stone gloss do not establish modern uses.

passage-zhongshan-r07-banshi.name: Mount Banshi
passage-zhongshan-r07-banshi.description: Seventy li east is Mount Banshi. Jiarong sprouts into ears and has red leaves and flowers but no fruit. Laixu water rises on the sunny side and flows west into the Yi, with Lun fish resembling fu and bearing black markings. He water rises on the shaded side and flows north into the Luo, with Teng fish, gui-like with blue-green markings and red tails. Guo Pu describes the growth sequence and, separately, gui fish with large mouths and eyes and fine scales. Channel dwelling supplies no legs; the medical claims are ancient.

passage-zhongshan-r07-summary.name: Seventh-range summary and rites
passage-zhongshan-r07-summary.description: The seventh range from Xiuyu to Dagui reports nineteen mountains and 1,184 li. Sixteen gods have pig bodies and human faces, with sheep offerings and buried multicolored jade. Ku, Shaoshi and Taishi are three distinguished peaks; their gods have human faces and three heads, with grand offerings and auspicious jade. The other gods remain pig-bodied and human-faced. Three heads do not specify a torso, so the image is a head study only. Ritual animals do not provide deity bodies; the original missing zhong marker stays in captured text.

passage-zhongshan-r08-jingshan.name: Mount Jingshan (northeast of Jing)
passage-zhongshan-r08-jingshan.description: A hundred li northeast is Mount Jingshan, with iron on its shaded side and red metal on its sunny side. It has li cattle, tigers and leopards, song and bai trees, bamboo, ju and you. Zhang water rises here and flows southeast into Ju water, with gold and Jiao fish; the text also lists lümi. Guo Pu describes li cattle as black mao-cattle kind and you as larger than ju, with thick peel and a sour taste. The Jiao gloss spans 300–301, describing patterned tough skin, a long tail and an ancient venom claim, without settling modern shark or ray identity. Lümi and its larger-than-deer comparison retain uncertain word division. Unit 297 is on scan 34, followed by scan 35.

passage-zhongshan-r08-jiao.description: A hundred and fifty li northeast is Mount Jiao, with jade above and qinghu below, and song, bai, taozhi and gouduan plants. The god Tuowei dwells here, with a human face, goat horns and tiger claws, wandering in the Sui-Zhang pool and giving light when entering or leaving. The torso and limb count are not given. The illustration is a partial anatomy study only: a human face with goat horns and separately presented tiger paws. Age, horn curvature, two-paw layout and neutral base are artistic. The light claim adds no flames, and the pool is not forcibly merged with earlier river names.

passage-zhongshan-r08-nvji.name: Mount Nüji
passage-zhongshan-r08-nvji.description: A hundred and twenty li northeast is Mount Nüji, with jade above and gold below. It lists leopards, tigers, lümi, jing and ji beasts, white Jiao birds, Zhai birds and Zhen birds. Guo Pu describes white Jiao as pheasant-like with long tails, walking and calling. The damaged Zhen glyph in unit 308 is restored from the scan in the reading layer only. Its gloss gives purple-green coloring, a long head and red bill, with male Yunmu and female Yinxie names as captured. Long-head and Yunmu readings are not changed to other editions; the feeding claim is not illustrated. Unit 306 is on scan 35, followed by scan 36.

passage-zhongshan-r08-lun.description: Three hundred and fifty li northeast is Mount Lun, with zi, nan, taozhi, zha, li, ju and you trees, and animals named lüchen, ling and chuo. passage-zhongshan-r08-summary.name: Eighth-range summary and rites
passage-zhongshan-r08-summary.description: The Jing range from Mount Jing to Qingu is reported as twenty-three mountains and 2,890 li. Its gods have bird bodies and human faces. General rites use a rooster, a zao-gui jade and tu grain; Mount Jiao has separate wine and lesser-livestock rites. The summary begins on scan 40 and continues on 41. General offerings and Jiao-specific rites remain separate. The deity image depicts a full bird body with a human face; feather pattern, species, age, colors and pose are artistic.

passage-zhongshan-r09-nvfan.name: Mount Nüfan
passage-zhongshan-r09-nvfan.description: The ninth Central range begins at Mount Nüfan, with stone nie, niu and jiang trees, ju and zhu herbs. Luo water rises here and flows east into the Jiang, with xionghuang in it; tigers and leopards are listed. Nüfan is retained as the opening mountain name. This east-flowing Luo-to-Jiang account is not forced into the earlier Yi/Luo river index. Guo Pu explicitly notes xionghuang occurring in water. Animal names supply no independent detailed forms.

passage-zhongshan-r09-min.name: Mount Min
passage-zhongshan-r09-min.description: Three hundred li northeast is Mount Min. Jiang water rises here and flows northeast into the sea, with fine turtles and Tuo. Gold and jade occur above, white min below, and mei and tang trees; xi beasts, elephants, Kui cattle, Han and Bi birds are listed. The Tuo gloss spans 359–360: lizard-like, large examples two zhang long, with patterned scales and a historical skin use. Kui cattle are described as large cattle in a historical account across 361–362, without a one-legged thunder-beast form. White Han and red Bi lack independent full anatomy.

passage-zhongshan-r09-lai.name: Mount Lai
passage-zhongshan-r09-lai.description: A hundred and forty li northeast is Mount Lai. Jiang water rises here and flows east into the Great Jiang. Gold occurs on its sunny side, mi and zhu animals on its shaded side, with tan and zhe trees, xie, jiu, yao and kongduo. Commentary calls this the southern Jiang source and records Mo at a nine-turn slope: bear-like, mottled black and white, with an ancient metal-eating claim. Mo is commentary evidence, not main text or a modern panda identification. Yao and kongduo glosses remain separate; a shed-skin gloss supplies no live monster anatomy.

passage-zhongshan-r09-fengyu.name: Mount Fengyu
passage-zhongshan-r09-fengyu.description: A hundred and fifty li east is Mount Fengyu, with white metal above, stone nie below, and zou, shan and yang trees. Xuanyu water flows east into the Jiang and has snakes. Animals include lümi, zhu, leopards and tigers; birds include white jiao. passage-zhongshan-r09-summary.description: The Min range is reported from Nüji to Jiachao as sixteen mountains and 3,500 li. Its gods have horse bodies and dragon heads. General rites use a rooster, burial and tu grain; Wen, Goumi, Fengyu and Chou have separate rites, and Xiong has wine, livestock, jade and dances. The summary names Nüji where the route begins with Nüfan, and includes Wen and Chou without forcing new route mountains. General and mountain-specific rites remain distinct; ritual animals are not deity anatomy.

passage-zhongshan-r10-summary.name: Tenth-range summary and rites
passage-zhongshan-r10-summary.description: The Shouyang range is reported from Shou to Bing as nine mountains and 267 li. Its gods have dragon bodies and human faces. General rites use a rooster, burial and five kinds of grain; Du and Gui have separate livestock, wine, jade and dance rites. The route distances total 310 li, distinct from the reported 267. Du and Gui lack separate route accounts in this range and are not imported from elsewhere. The final rites span scans 49–50.

passage-zhongshan-r11-yiwang.name: Mount Yiwang
passage-zhongshan-r11-yiwang.description: The eleventh Central range, Jing, begins at Mount Yiwang. Tuan water flows east into the Ji; Kuang water flows southeast into the Han and has Jiao. Song and bai grow above, lacquer and zi below, with red metal on the sunny side and min on the shaded side. Commentary describes Jiao as snake-like with four feet, a small head, thin neck and white neck swelling; the image adds no horns or wings. The historical Tuan-to-Qing route remains separate from the main-text Ji recipient.

passage-zhongshan-r11-feng-first.name: Mount Feng (first eleventh-range account)
passage-zhongshan-r11-feng-first.description: Three hundred li southeast is Mount Feng. Yonghe resembles an ape, with red eyes, a red muzzle and a yellow body, and is an ancient fear omen. Gengfu frequents the Qingling pool, entering and leaving with light, with an ancient defeat omen. Nine bells respond to frost; gold lies above and gu, zuo, niu and jiang grow below. The first Feng account spans scans 51–52 and stays separate from its later namesake. Yonghe limb proportions and pose are artistic; Gengfu has no supplied body form. The bells are objects, not additional creatures.

passage-zhongshan-r11-cong.name: Mount Cong
passage-zhongshan-r11-cong.description: Thirty-five li southeast is Mount Cong, with song and bai above and bamboo below. Cong water emerges above and disappears below, with three-footed softshell turtles with branching tails, said to avert harmful afflictions and epidemics when eaten. The commentary calls the three-footed turtle Neng and cites Erya across units 479–480. Three legs and a split tail follow the text; limb arrangement, shell texture, colors and pose are artistic. No six-eyed comparison is imported.

passage-zhongshan-r11-xuan.description: Fifty li east is Mount Xuan. Lun water flows southeast into Shi water and has Jiao. A mulberry called Dinü has a size of fifty chi, four-way branches, leaves over one chi, red markings, yellow flowers and blue-green fu. The fu body-part remains unresolved and supplies no deity portrait. The account spans scans 57–58.

passage-zhongshan-r11-summary.name: Eleventh-range summary and rites
passage-zhongshan-r11-summary.description: The Jing range from Yiwang to Ji is reported as forty-eight mountains and 3,732 li. Its gods have pig bodies and human heads. General rites use a rooster, prayer and burial, a gui jade and five kinds of refined grain. He has imperial rites, and Du and Yu have separate principal-mountain rites. The captured cattle wording is not assigned a fixed number. He, Du and Yu are not inserted as extra route mountains. Pig bodies and human heads inform the image; four hooves, hair, colors and pose are artistic. The passage spans scans 61–62.

passage-zhongshan-r12-dongting.name: Mount Dongting
passage-zhongshan-r12-dongting.description: A hundred and twenty li southeast is Mount Dongting, with gold above, silver and iron below, zha, li, ju and you trees, and jian, miwu, shaoyao and xiongqiong herbs. Two daughters of the Di dwell here and frequent the Jiang pool; Li-Yuan winds connect with the Xiaoxiang pool among the Nine Jiang, with whirling wind and torrential rain. Strange gods resemble people, carrying snakes and holding snakes in both hands; strange birds also occur. Guo Pu’s long commentary cites Yao-daughter and Shun-consort accounts and then disputes their conflation with the two deities. Those cited claims, his argument and the main text remain separate. No portraits of the daughters are invented. The strange-god image chooses one shoulder-carried snake plus one in each hand; carried count, placement, clothing and appearance are artistic. The archaic rain character is read as bao, while its captured marker is retained. This passage spans scans 64–65, including every commentary-only block.

passage-zhongshan-r12-bao.description: A hundred and eighty li southeast is Mount Bao, with zong, nan, jing and qi growth and several named bamboos; gold and jade above, patterned stone and iron below, and mi, deer, jun and jiu in its animal list. passage-zhongshan-r12-summary.name: Twelfth-range summary and rites
passage-zhongshan-r12-summary.description: The Dongting range from Pianyu to Rongyu is reported as fifteen mountains and 2,800 li. Its gods have bird bodies and dragon heads. General rites use a rooster, a female pig, cutting rites and tu grain; Fufu, Jigong, Yao and Yangdi have separate principal-mountain rites, while Dongting and Rongyu have wine, greater livestock, gui and bi jades and colored decoration. The individually stated route distances total 1,849 li, distinct from the reported 2,800. Ritual groups remain separate; offerings are not deity anatomy. Full bird bodies and dragon heads inform the image; legs, wings, tails, colors and pose are artistic.

passage-zhongshan-yu-cosmography.name: Yu’s cosmography and resources of the state
passage-zhongshan-yu-cosmography.description: Yu says the renowned mountains number 5,370 and occupy 64,056 li, describing the five repositories while omitting numerous smaller mountains. Heaven and earth extend 28,000 li east to west and 26,000 north to south; water-emitting mountains and water-receiving mountains are each reported in 8,000 li. Copper-producing mountains number 467 and iron-producing mountains 3,690. These lands sustain grain and supply spears, lances, knives and sha weapons. The capable have a surplus and the unskilled lack enough. Seventy-two houses performed feng rites at Tai and shan rites at Liangfu; gains and losses lie within this account, called the resources of the state. These are textual cosmographic, resource and political claims, not modern survey data or weapon-making instructions. Counts and li remain separate; the five repositories refer to the text, not human organs. The scan neng character is restored only in the reading layer. The final Guanzi gloss spans scans 69–70.
